note: Datasets FPR could add to the observatory, each a candidate: the source, license, coverage and terms still have to be confirmed before anything is harvested. Status moves from candidate to checked (tested by request, see 'check'), building, live or blocked (with the reason and who to ask). Every row has a domain from the domain registry (dictionary_src/domains.json): 'domain' is the primary one and 'domains' lists the primary first, then secondary ones. Edit this file (or add a row) and rebuild; the chat reads it to answer what is missing.
domain_note: The 'theme' field is the older grouping the chat still reads; it will be replaced by 'domain' when the chat moves to the registry.

items.title: Business establishments by industry and size (County Business Patterns)
items.why: Fills the cells the jobs data withholds and shows how many small firms each municipality has, which employment counts hide.
items.source: US Census Bureau
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.check: Confirm Puerto Rico municipio coverage and the latest year; some cells are withheld or given as ranges.

items.title: Self-employed businesses with no employees (Nonemployer Statistics)
items.why: A window on the informal and micro-business economy that payroll data cannot see, and where it is concentrated.
items.source: US Census Bureau
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.check: Confirm municipio detail for Puerto Rico and how recent it is.

items.title: Paycheck Protection Program loans (2020-2021)
items.why: Which municipalities and industries received pandemic support, set against jobs and tourism.
items.source: US Small Business Administration
items.check: Large file; confirm the municipio field is complete. Borrower names are public, but only aggregates are needed.

items.title: Economic Census (sales, payroll, firms by industry)
items.why: Sales and value added by industry, not just jobs: shows where the money is made.
items.source: US Census Bureau
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.check: Confirm the latest census year available for municipios.

items.title: Gross domestic product of Puerto Rico
items.why: The island-wide economic output to set the municipal jobs and wages against. Island-level only, not by municipality.
items.source: US Bureau of Economic Analysis
items.check: Locate the current territory GDP tables.

items.title: Bank deposits by branch (Summary of Deposits)
items.why: Where savings and banking access are, and where branches have closed: a proxy for local financial health.
items.source: FDIC
items.check: Published 2026-11-16 (decision 107, step 4; credit.py, docs/credit.md): bank offices and their deposits by municipio, June 30 of each year 2000-2026, in credit_series.json. Puerto Rico had 571 offices in 2006 and 260 in 2026. No office points: since 2023 the FDIC places about half the offices at the centre of their ZIP code (113 of 260 have a street-level location), so a map would put banks where they are not; geocoding the addresses is left for step 6. Cooperativas (COSSEC) are not in the file.

items.title: Agriculture: farms, acreage and sales (Census of Agriculture)
items.why: Food-system and rural-economy layer; links to land use and hurricane damage.
items.source: USDA NASS
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05: the 2022 Census of Agriculture for Puerto Rico is published for the island and six regions only, as PDF; NASS QuickStats needs a key. A keyless alternative at municipio level is the NRCS prime-farmland soils (see the farmland row).

items.title: Night-time lights (satellite)
items.why: A monthly, fine-grained proxy for economic activity and power restoration after storms, below the municipality.
items.source: NASA Black Marble (VNP46A3 monthly, collection 2), LAADS DAAC
items.licence: NASA data: CC0 unless marked otherwise; cite the data (NASA data use guidance)
items.geography: Raster, 15 arc-seconds (about 460 m); summaries for barrios and municipios
items.check: Checked 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02: the Earth Observation Group's files redirect to a sign-in, and NASA Black Marble (VNP46A3 monthly, collection 2) is listed openly on LAADS but a download without a login gets HTTP 303 to a sign-in page. Live 2026-11-04: nightlights_series.json and nightlights_barrio.json (mean radiance and the share of poor-quality pixels, 2012-2025, by municipio and barrio) and nightlights_monthly.json (2012-01 to 2026-09), built by nightlights.py with a free NASA Earthdata token used only by the build (HANDOFF decision 75).

items.title: Hotel occupancy, room rates and guest arrivals (PRTC monthly report)
items.why: Demand to set against the tourism supply on the map: where capacity is used and where it is not.
items.source: Puerto Rico Tourism Company (through the Instituto de Estadísticas and tourism.pr.gov)
items.licence: Not stated; the PRTC site footer says all rights reserved
items.geography: Tourism region (Metro and 5 others), hotel size class; no municipio, no hotel level
items.cadence: Monthly (PRTC PDF to 2026-06); Instituto spreadsheets stop at 2024-12 and skip months
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05. The monthly Registration and Occupancy workbook (Dec 2024 file, 0.7 MB) gives arrivals, non-resident share, occupancy, room-nights sold and available, daily rate and stay length by region and by hotel size; the PRTC site has a 41-page PDF through Jun 2026. Region membership by municipio is on the PRTC regions page and as 78 polygons in the island geoserver. Missing: municipio, property level, room counts. Ask PRTC for machine-readable monthly files and for the reuse terms.

items.title: Airport passengers and flights (FAA, BTS and Ports Authority)
items.why: How many people enter each gateway, by month, to set against hotel capacity, ground transport and jobs.
items.source: FAA (enplanements), BTS (T-100), Puerto Rico Ports Authority and Tourism Company
items.licence: US Government work, public domain (FAA, BTS); Ports Authority report is free to distribute, no license stated
items.geography: Airport (8 in the FAA file, 7 in T-100, 10 in the Ports Authority report)
items.cadence: FAA yearly (CY2025 final 2026-09); BTS monthly (to 2026-04); Ports Authority monthly (PRTC PDF to 2026-07)
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05, keyless. FAA CY2025 file (58 KB) lists 8 Puerto Rico airports: San Juan 6,658,037 enplanements, Aguadilla 335,014, Ponce 95,055, Vieques 35,973, Ceiba 23,214, Culebra 19,812, Isla Grande 17,466, Mayagüez 8,991. BTS T-100 origin summary gives monthly passengers for 7 airports, Jan 2014 to Apr 2026 (San Juan 6,687,309 in 2025); FAA and BTS agree within about 1% (Culebra within 2%). Ceiba is only in the FAA file. The PRTC/Ports Authority report adds arrivals and departures separately for San Juan, Aguadilla and Ponce to Jul 2026, and 10 airports in the quarterly workbook. To confirm: why San Juan 'out' counts (6.82 million in 2025) exceed enplanements. Live 2026-10-14: gateway_series.json, air passengers boarding and commercial flights departing for each municipality 2014-2025 (BTS T-100) and FAA enplanements 2023-2025 (with Ceiba). The PRTC/Ports Authority arrivals and the San Juan 'out' question remain open.

items.title: Cruise ship calls and passengers (Old San Juan and Ponce)
items.why: A large, concentrated visitor flow into Old San Juan that hotel data do not capture, and the piers where ground transport has to meet it.
items.source: Puerto Rico Tourism Company, San Juan Cruise Port, Puerto Rico Ports Authority, BTS
items.licence: Not stated; the PRTC site footer says all rights reserved
items.geography: Port (Old San Juan piers; Ponce a few calls a year)
items.cadence: Monthly (PRTC PDF); yearly (San Juan Cruise Port, BTS)
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05. PRTC publishes monthly passengers and calls for Old San Juan, homeport versus in transit, by calendar and fiscal year (PDF): 2025 was 1,615,039 passengers and 563 calls. San Juan Cruise Port shows 1,593,513 passengers and 561 calls for 2025 (HTML, yearly back to 2008). BTS has 2023 only (San Juan 438 calls, 1,303,648 passengers). No split by pier; a Ports Authority PDF names Piers 1, 3 and 4 and Pan American I and II. Ask PRTC for spreadsheets and whether future months in the PDF are scheduled calls. The old url (pports.org) does not resolve; the authority's site is prpa.pr.gov.

items.title: National Risk Index (expected annual loss, social vulnerability, resilience)
items.why: Compares hurricane, flood, earthquake, landslide and other risk across municipios, with community resilience, next to the economy and housing layers.
items.source: FEMA
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: expected annual loss $3.19 billion a year (hurricane 1.48 B, earthquake 0.80 B, inland flood 0.31 B, landslide 0.29 B). The composite risk score, social vulnerability and resilience are empty for Puerto Rico: say so on the page and use the resilience-estimates and SVI rows instead. Live 2026-10-14 (Phase 3 item 11): environment_series.json, expected annual loss in all and for six hazards for each municipio (December 2025). The composite score, social vulnerability and resilience are still empty for Puerto Rico and are not published.

items.title: Earthquakes (2019-2020 southwest sequence and ongoing)
items.why: Locates the seismic zone against housing age, schools and the economy of the southwest.
items.source: USGS ComCat earthquake catalogue
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 12,507 events in the 2019-2020 southwest sequence. Use magnitude 2.5 or more and page the requests by year. Live 2026-10-14 (Phase 3 item 11): hazard_series.json, earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more and 4.0 or more placed in or off each municipio every year, 2000-2025.

items.title: Hurricane tracks (live through the 2025 season); wind swaths not added
items.why: Shows which municipalities took which storm, to read recovery money and damage against.
items.source: NOAA National Hurricane Center HURDAT2
items.cadence: Annual (NHC file for the 2025 season dated 2026-09-23)
items.check: Live: 157 storms within 250 km of the island, 1851 to 2025 (the 2026-10 snapshot; build looks up the newest NHC file with --refresh). Wind swaths and the IBTrACS archive are not added.

items.title: Landslide susceptibility and inventory
items.why: Mountain-municipality hazard that the flood layer misses, tied to roads and housing.
items.source: UPRM mirror of the USGS landslide inventory after Hurricane Maria; USGS landslide susceptibility raster
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 71,431 inventory points with municipio and barrio (barrio names have typos: count by point in polygon). The USGS susceptibility raster is a 5 m raster in a 290 MB zip: a one-time job to compute the percent of each municipio at high index. The inventory is a mirror: say so. Partly live 2026-10-14 (Phase 3 item 11): environment_series.json, landslides mapped after Hurricane María for each municipio (read from the first author's copy at UPRM). The susceptibility raster is not built: the build has no raster reader yet. Live 2026-10-18: landslide_series.json and landslide_barrio.json (landslide.py, docs/landslide.md) give the share of land in each class, in the high-or-above and very-high-or-above classes, and the 2020 residents in the high-or-above classes, for every barrio and municipio of the main island. The USGS data release (doi 10.5066/P990ZP4C, CC0) sits on ScienceBase, which refuses scripts, so the build reads the first author's tile copy at UPRM (zoom 15, about 4.5 m) and checks it against the report's class areas and table 5.

items.title: Tide gauges and coastal water levels
items.why: Measured, live sea level against the modelled sea-level-rise layer.
items.source: NOAA CO-OPS tide gauges
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 13 gauges in Puerto Rico.

items.title: River gauges and rainfall
items.why: Live flood signals by watershed, set against the flood-zone map and exposed places.
items.source: USGS streamgages (new water data API), NOAA Atlas 14 rainfall, NOAA GHCN stations
items.check: Live 2026-11-11: the River flow layer draws the 71 USGS stream gauges that report now and have 8 years of record (river_gauges.geojson, river_gauges.py), with the latest reading asked of USGS in the visitor's browser. Still wanted: rainfall (NOAA Atlas 14 frequencies, GHCN stations) and the National Weather Service's flood stages for the gauges that have them. Verified 2026-10-05: 7,318 stream-measurement locations, 285 GHCN stations, and Atlas 14 rainfall frequencies are available without a key.

items.title: Electric service by municipio and district: batteries, sales, smart meters, rooftop solar and reliability (LUMA filings at the Energy Bureau)
items.why: Where homes now store and make their own power, where electricity is used, and how reliable the service is, by place.
items.source: LUMA Energy, monthly metrics workbook and quarterly distributed generation exhibits filed with the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau
items.licence: No licence stated; public filings with the Energy Bureau (energia.pr.gov states no terms of use; LUMA's own website bars automated access and is not used)
items.geography: Municipio (batteries, sales, smart meters); 34 LUMA commercial districts (rooftop solar); 16 technical districts (SAIDI)
items.check: Checked 2026-11-13 (HANDOFF decision 104): LUMA's own site bars scripts, but the same reports are public filings at energia.pr.gov, keyless. 'Resumen-Metricas-Master_<Month><Year>.xlsx' (case NEPR-MI-2019-0007, sheet T&D) has, monthly from June 2021: battery installations and kWh, electricity sales (GWh) and the share of customers on smart meters for each municipio (San Juan split into San Juan, Río Piedras and Santurce), rooftop solar MW and installations for 34 commercial districts (1,666.2 MW and 209,404 installations in September 2026; 189,459 batteries, 3.15 GWh) and SAIDI for 16 technical districts. The distributed generation exhibits (case NEPR-MI-2019-0016, quarterly) give a monthly series from 2010 (1,621.6 MW in June 2026); file names vary, so a script reads the case page. Decision 104 (d) approved reading them by script. Outage events by place are in LUMA's FY SAIDI/SAIFI workbook (73 MB).

items.title: Drinking water service and interruptions
items.why: Service reliability by place next to poverty and age.
items.source: EPA ECHO drinking water systems and NPDES permits (PRASA interruptions are a separate, blocked row)
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 402 active community water systems serve 3.29 million people; 248 have a current violation flag. A violation flag is a compliance record, not proof the water is unsafe. Aggregate small private operators. Partly live 2026-10-14 (Phase 3 item 10): community water systems, health-based violations and enforcement priority for each municipality (EPA ECHO, infrastructure_series.json). Interruptions are still not open (prasa-interruptions). Since 2026-10-18 also the systems outside PRASA (non-PRASA, privately owned in SDWIS) and the residents they report serving, by municipality; their locations by barrio are not public (non-prasa-locations).

items.title: Broadband availability and speeds
items.why: Goes beyond the survey's household internet share to the infrastructure itself.
items.source: FCC Broadband Data Collection (National Broadband Map), public data API
items.geography: Location, summed by census block to barrio and municipio
items.cadence: Twice a year (the June release is used)
items.check: Live 2026-11-10 (HANDOFF decision 94): the API answers with FPR's FCC account (secrets FCC_BDC_USERNAME and FCC_BDC_HASH, GitHub Actions only). broadband_series.json and broadband_barrio.json: locations, BEAD tiers and fiber, June 2023-2026. Without an account the map answers 403 and the API 401.

items.title: Health professional shortage areas (HRSA); underserved areas (MUA/P) not published
items.why: Access to care by municipality against age, poverty and travel time.
items.source: HRSA
items.licence: US Government work; HRSA's download page lists no usage limitations
items.check: Live (2026-10-06): the area-level shortage designations of each municipio for primary care (20 municipios), dental (77) and mental health (52), as priority score, practitioners still needed and percent of need met, in health_series.json (health_series.py, docs/health.md). Checked against HRSA's Designated HPSA Quarterly Summary (as of 2026-09-30): the populations of designated areas agree exactly and the practitioners needed are each within 1.1%. Facility designations are left out. Medically underserved areas are not published: the 72 Puerto Rico designations are all dated 1978 and the underservice score has no inputs (0.00 for 71, 50.00 for one); six municipios have none.

items.title: School locations, enrolment and closures
items.why: School consolidation against population decline and commuting.
items.source: NCES Common Core of Data and EDGE school locations; Urban Institute Education Data Portal (mirror of the CCD)
items.licence: NCES: US Government work, public domain. Urban Institute mirror: ODC-By 1.0 (credit the source).
items.cadence: Annual (CCD back to 1986-87; EDGE one layer per year)
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 865 Puerto Rico schools in 2024-25 (855 open, 3 closed) with coordinates in EDGE; enrolment by school 1995-2024 through the Urban mirror (627,620 in 1995, 235,819 in 2024); closures by year from the EDGE year layers (1,329 schools in 2016-17, 847 in 2019-20). CCD files have no coordinates: join to EDGE. Re-test the URLs the day you build. Not in the exposure series yet: plan item 5 (built 2026-10-06; exposure.py, docs/exposure.md) covers flood, sea level rise, protected land and transit stops only. Once the points are harvested, add a distance family (residents and housing units within a stated distance of a point) in exposure.py (docs/exposure.md, section 8); the existing files do not change. Live 2026-10-14 (Phase 3 item 8): education_series.json has public schools open, students, teachers, students per teacher and closures for each municipality, every school year 2010-2024, through the Urban mirror; school points are not published.

items.title: Fatal traffic crashes
items.why: Road danger by place and mode, next to the transit and commuting layers.
items.source: NHTSA Fatality Analysis Reporting System (FARS)
items.geography: Municipio (from 2020), counts only; Puerto Rico totals since 2015
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 275 fatal crashes in 2024. Publish counts by municipio and year only: the exact date, time and place of a death can identify a person. Live 2026-11-13 (decision 105, step 3): NHTSA's Puerto Rico FARS files 2015-2024 (2024 first release); crashes_series.json gives fatal crashes, deaths, pedestrians and bicyclists, motorcyclists, deaths per 100,000 residents and per 100 million vehicle-km; the deaths along each simulated connection as five-year totals. No crash is drawn.

items.title: Workers who travel between municipios (Census commuting flows)
items.why: Where people travel to work, to set against the transit routes: the origin-destination data the transit analysis lacked.
items.source: US Census Bureau, County-to-County Commuting Flows (American Community Survey)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-13 without a key: 1,626 one-way flows between municipios, 532,691 workers, each with a margin of error. Live 2026-11-13 (decision 105): transit_links.json, the Knowledge Area page Connections between municipios and the layer Simulated connections between municipios.

items.title: Road traffic volumes and condition
items.why: Where congestion and heavy use are, against jobs and commute times.
items.source: FHWA Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS)
items.geography: Road segment (main roads drawn) and municipio aggregates
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 180,776 Puerto Rico segments in the 2024 data, about 90 calls to read them. Publish municipio aggregates. The layer also carries AADT by vehicle class, functional class, lanes, speed limit, signals and terrain, and pavement condition fields (IRI, PSR, rutting, faulting, cracking, surface type); whether the condition fields are filled for Puerto Rico was not tested. Live 2026-11-13 (decision 105, step 2): FHWA's HPMS_FULL_PR_2025 on geo.dot.gov (262,462 sections); the layer Traffic on the main roads (3,829 stretches) and six municipio figures in traffic_series.json, among them rough pavement by IRI (the condition fields are filled on the main roads).

items.title: Real-time bus, train and ferry positions
items.why: The live layer the transit tab cannot yet show.
items.source: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado
items.check: Rechecked 2026-10-05: ATI's open data page (published 2026-08-10) still says GTFS-RT is in development; the MobilityData catalog lists 1,929 real-time feeds and none for Puerto Rico. Ferry tracking and arrival times exist only in the City Experiences app, and bus positions only in the AMA Móvil app. ATI's Llame y Viaje is eligibility-based paratransit, not a visitor service.
items.who_to_ask: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (planning office); Hornblower (Puerto Rico Ferry) for the ferry app data

items.title: Building footprints and heights
items.why: Counts and sizes of buildings by barrio: housing stock, exposure to flood and the 3D view.
items.source: Overture Maps buildings theme (OpenStreetMap, Google Open Buildings and Microsoft footprints, conflated), release 2026-10-21.0
items.licence: ODbL 1.0 (Open Database License): credit Overture Maps Foundation and OpenStreetMap contributors; derived databases stay ODbL
items.size: large (store counts per barrio, not footprints)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-09 without a key. Puerto Rico (Mona to Culebra) has 2,157,363 buildings in release 2026-10-21.0: 1,500,399 from OpenStreetMap (the ones the 3D view already draws from the OpenFreeMap base map), 536,571 from Google and 120,393 from Microsoft. Only 203,060 (9.4%) have a height and 8,499 a number of floors. Overture's own PMTiles for the release (tiles/2026-10-21.0/buildings.pmtiles on the overturemaps-extras-us-west-2 bucket, 180 GB worldwide) answer range requests from any website (CORS *), but Overture says these tiles are for inspection, not production, and each release has a new path. Proposal: docs/geoai-sources-proposal-2026-11.md (decision 91). Private homes: shapes only, no value per building; counts and sizes by barrio. Live 2026-11-09 (decision 91, step A1): buildings_series.json and buildings_barrio.json by buildings.py: the number of buildings, buildings per km², land under roofs, the median footprint, buildings in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area (count and share) and the share traced by machine learning, by barrio and municipio (2,157,028 placed; 9.0% in a Special Flood Hazard Area; Spearman 0.965 with 2020 housing units across barrios). 2026-11-10 (A2): the 3D view also draws the buildings OpenStreetMap lacks, from buildings_gap.pmtiles (buildings3d.py; 704,061 at zoom 14, 7.4 MB). Hosting measured first: Overture's own tiles for Puerto Rico are 153.5 MB, every building slimmed 29.0 MB, the missing ones alone 7.4 MB, on GitHub Pages.

items.title: Building heights for every building (GlobalBuildingAtlas)
items.why: Overture has a height for fewer than 1 in 10 buildings in Puerto Rico. A modelled height for each one would give true 3D massing, floor area by barrio and shade for the heat work.
items.source: GlobalBuildingAtlas (Technical University of Munich), heights and LoD1 models, reference year 2019
items.licence: Polygons ODbL; heights and LoD1 models CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial): Compliance to confirm FPR's use
items.size: large (5-degree tiles; store heights joined to the Overture footprints, or summaries)
items.check: 2026-11-09: the licence of the heights and LoD1 models is CC BY-NC 4.0 on the Hugging Face card (zhu-xlab/GBA.LoD1); polygons are a separate ODbL set. Still to check: Puerto Rico's tile, height error against the 3DEP lidar (surface minus terrain), and Compliance on non-commercial use.

items.title: Land cover change (forest, urban, agriculture)
items.why: Urban growth and forest loss over time, set against population and protected areas.
items.source: MRLC tree canopy (2011-2021) and NOAA C-CAP land cover (2010)
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: tree canopy 2011-2021 (for example El Yunque 91% to 87%) and C-CAP land cover for 2010 only. There is no land-cover change series for Puerto Rico; label them as snapshots. 2026-10-14: not built in item 11. Canopy and land cover are rasters and the build has no raster reader yet.

items.title: Land cover every year, 10 m (Esri / Impact Observatory, 2017-2023)
items.why: A yearly land cover series where the island has only snapshots: forest, crops, built area and bare ground before and after María, by municipio and barrio.
items.source: Impact Observatory and Esri, 10 m Annual Land Use Land Cover (9 classes) V2, from Microsoft Planetary Computer (io-lulc-annual-v02)
items.geography: Raster, 10 m (publish barrio and municipio summaries)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-09 without a key: 14 tiles over Puerto Rico, years 2017 to 2023, read by raster.py (UTM 20N, nodata 0). Modelled from Sentinel-2 by machine learning: compare the built-area class with the Overture footprints and the forest class with the MRLC canopy before publishing, and say that year-to-year changes include model noise.

items.title: Land cover 2020 and 2021, 10 m (ESA WorldCover)
items.why: A second, independent land cover map for the same years, to show where the models agree before the yearly series is trusted.
items.source: European Space Agency WorldCover v100 (2020) and v200 (2021), from Microsoft Planetary Computer (esa-worldcover)
items.geography: Raster, 10 m (used as a check; summaries only)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-09 without a key: tile N18W069 (2021) read by raster.py (EPSG:4326). Use as a quality check of landcover-annual, not as its own layer.

items.title: Tree cover loss by year since 2001 (Hansen / Global Forest Watch)
items.why: Where and in which year tree cover was lost, 2001 to 2024: María's damage in 2017, then regrowth or clearing, by barrio and against protected areas.
items.source: University of Maryland, Hansen Global Forest Change v1.12 (2000-2024), the data behind Global Forest Watch
items.check: Verified 2026-11-09 without a key: tile 20N_070W downloads, but it is a striped GeoTIFF, which raster.py refuses. Either add strip reading to raster.py (the strip index works with range requests like tiles) or download the tile once into the cache. Hurricane damage counts as loss even where trees regrow: label it tree cover loss, not deforestation.

items.title: Building permits
items.why: New construction as an early signal of where growth and investment are going.
items.source: US Census Bureau Building Permits Survey, or the island permit office
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.check: Confirm whether Puerto Rico municipios are covered and in what detail.

items.title: Disaster recovery spending by municipality and program
items.why: Money obligated versus spent, set against damage and need, so delays show up on the map.
items.source: COR3 and the Housing Department (CDBG-DR) reports
items.check: Federal grant data: Finance and Compliance review before any external use. Locate the official reports and their terms. 2026-10-30: the FEMA part is live from OpenFEMA (row fema-recovery): Public Assistance by damage category and Hazard Mitigation approved, obligated and awaiting decision. COR3 and CDBG-DR reports are still to locate. USAspending places 100% of the prime awards of FEMA Public Assistance, Hazard Mitigation and CDBG-DR in San Juan (FY2019 and FY2024 checked), so it cannot give a municipal map of them.

items.title: FEMA Public Assistance by damage category, and Hazard Mitigation Assistance
items.why: What FEMA's recovery money repairs (roads, buildings, utilities) and how much mitigation money was approved, obligated or is still awaiting a decision, by municipio.
items.source: FEMA, OpenFEMA (PublicAssistanceFundedProjectsDetails v2, HmaSubapplications v2)
items.licence: US Government work; OpenFEMA terms apply
items.geography: Municipio (applicant for Public Assistance, benefiting municipio for Hazard Mitigation); a large part is statewide
items.cadence: Updated daily by FEMA; refreshed with each snapshot
items.check: Live 2026-10-30 (Public money v2, step 1): economy_series.json, eight damage categories and Section 406 mitigation (23,052 projects; 77.9% of the federal share is statewide, 99.9% of utilities for 2017) and Hazard Mitigation approved, obligated, awaiting decision and approved subapplications (1,134 subapplications). Payments are not published: FEMA reports them for only 163 subapplications. Under the Compliance hold of the Public money series (HANDOFF decision 21).

items.title: Municipal and public finance (what exists)
items.why: How much each municipality can fund itself, which shapes what recovery and tourism projects it can carry.
items.source: Puerto Rico Comptroller and the municipal revenue centre (CRIM)
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05: the Census of Governments excludes Puerto Rico; Oversight Board plans are PDFs published 'as is'. The Comptroller contract registry runs from fiscal 2012-13 to 2022-23, has no license and holds contractor names (personal data): aggregates only, with written permission. See the blocked governance rows.

items.title: Colleges and universities (IPEDS)
items.why: Where postsecondary campuses are and how enrolment has changed, beside population and jobs.
items.source: NCES IPEDS
items.check: Verified 2026-10-05: 129 Puerto Rico institutions; fall enrolment 270,914 in 2010 and 167,883 in 2023. Drop administrator names and phone numbers (personal data). items.title: FBI Crime Data Explorer
items.why: Reported crime totals for Puerto Rico.
items.source: FBI Uniform Crime Reporting Program
items.check: Checked 2026-10-06. The API needs a key (the api.data.gov DEMO_KEY answers, 10 requests an hour). Puerto Rico is one agency with no municipio and no coordinates, and it does not report to NIBRS, so nothing below island level exists and the NIBRS by-state download has no Puerto Rico. The summary series has one value a year, none for 2015 to 2017. From 2021 violent crime equals homicide (2018: 6,417 violent and 639 homicides; 2021: 616 and 616; 2024: 488 and 488), while the API still reports 100% population coverage; read the drop as a reporting change, not a fall in crime (inference, not confirmed with the FBI). A keyless 'U.S. Territory Data' CSV is listed on the downloads page; not downloaded or inspected. Island-wide homicides are the only usable series. Municipio counts are live from the Police's own reports (police-type1 row); for barrio detail, see the police-incidents row.

items.title: Ferry itineraries, fares and boarding rules (Cataño, Vieques, Culebra)
items.why: Tells you when and at what cost a visitor can reach Old San Juan, Vieques and Culebra by boat, and what limits access: resident priority, no rental cars on board, one-hour check-in.
items.source: Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and Puerto Rico Ferry (Hornblower)
items.licence: Not stated; itineraries are PDFs and the site footer says all rights reserved
items.geography: Route and terminal (Cataño, Old San Juan, Ceiba, Vieques x2, Culebra)
items.cadence: Seasonal itineraries (current one runs 2026-08-01 to 2026-11-30); fares by regulation
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05. The only machine-readable schedule is the ATI GTFS (4 ferry routes, 6 stops, 385 trips). Its Cataño first and last departures and its Vieques weekday times match the official PDFs (apart from a Tuesday and Friday 3:45 AM departure that only the PDF notes and a Sunday 23:30 Cataño departure that only the feed has); Culebra (all days) and Vieques weekend departures do not, run times are placeholders (45 minutes for Culebra against 90 on the operator page) and island fares are missing. Fares in the ATI regulation: non-residents pay 11.25 USD per trip (residents 2.00 Vieques, 2.25 Culebra) plus a 2 USD conservation fee; news says the rise took effect 2026-05-05, while the portal rates page still shows resident prices. Vehicles board only if owned by island residents. Still to confirm with ATI: the fare in force, the itinerary after 2026-11-30 and a corrected GTFS.

items.geography: Route segment, terminal and vessel (6 terminals, 6 main route segments)
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05, keyless. Operator 'HMS Puerto Rico Ferry' has 6 terminals, 8 operator-segment rows and 24 vessels (10 in service). 2024 census passengers, both directions: Ceiba-Vieques 641,183, Ceiba-Culebra 546,258, Cataño-Old San Juan 428,604 (the 2020 census gave 530,295, 477,704 and 631,179 for 2019). In-service vessels carry 72 to 574 passengers; Isla Bonita (401) and Cayo Largo (297) serve the island routes. Average trip times 12, 60 and 90 minutes. Terminal link flags are self-reported. The file does not state its reference year; confirm in the BTS data dictionary. Live 2026-10-14: gateway_series.json, ferry passengers boarding at the terminals of each municipality for 2019, 2022 and 2024 (the 2020 census gives data year 2019; since 2022 BTS names a census for its data year). Vessels, trips and terminal links are not published yet.

The airport card (PDF image, 2023-12) repeats the zone fares and adds a 3 USD airport fee, 1 USD late-night and 1 USD per extra bag. The tables sit in a 5 MB PDF and must be keyed in by hand. Confirm with NTSP that the 2022 table is still in force.

items.title: National Walkability Index (EPA), by block group
items.why: A ready measure of how walkable the surroundings of a place are (intersection density, transit proximity, land-use mix), to temper straight-line walking distances.
items.source: US Environmental Protection Agency, Smart Location Database
items.licence: No license text in the service metadata; EPA is a US agency (confirm)
items.geography: Census block group (2019 boundaries), 2,552 in Puerto Rico
items.check: Checked 2026-10-05, keyless: all 2,552 Puerto Rico block groups have a walkability score (range 1 to 7.3, mean 4.7), plus intersection density, distance to transit, job-household mix and car-free household counts (183 fields; take about 10). Built on 2019 block groups and older input data. The street data behind the index may be licensed commercial data, so read the SLD user guide before republishing. Join to the observatory's 2020 blocks by area. Checked again 2026-11-14 for decision 107, step 2: the index is not usable for Puerto Rico. Three of its four parts are blank there: for all 2,552 block groups the ranks for employment and household mix (D2A_Ranked), employment mix (D2B_Ranked) and distance to transit (D4A_Ranked) are 1, the lowest, and total employment (TotEmp) is 0, because the jobs data behind the index (LEHD) does not cover Puerto Rico and no transit feed was read for it. Only intersection density varies, so the 'index' is that one measure rescaled, on 2019 block groups. Not published. The observatory can measure walkability itself from its own road network, timetables and places.

items.source: US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD eGIS)
items.licence: U.S. Public Domain (HUD open data catalog)
items.check: Built 2026-10-17 (facilities.py): 304 developments and 54,094 units counted by municipio; the 172 developments HUD geocoded to the rooftop or the ZIP+4 centroid are drawn, as HUD says to map. The housing authority's telephone, e-mail and director in HUD's layer are never requested.

items.title: Tax-exempt organizations (IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File)
items.why: How many nonprofits each municipio has, and in which fields, for civil-society and philanthropy planning.
items.source: Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
items.licence: US federal government work (public domain); the IRS page states no licence
items.check: Built 2026-10-17 (nonprofits.py): 2,572 organizations in the Puerto Rico file of 2026-10-13, counted by municipio, 501(c)(3) and NTEE major group. Names, EINs and addresses are never kept. Organizations registered only under Puerto Rico law are not in the file.

items.title: Where the community water systems outside PRASA (non-PRASA) are, by barrio or sector
items.why: Non-PRASA systems serve rural communities in the mountains; their location by barrio would show who depends on them and who is exposed when they fail.
items.source: EPA Region 2 Caribbean Environmental Protection Division, non-PRASA systems database (2022-2024 assessments, with geocoordinates); Puerto Rico Department of Health, Drinking Water Program
items.licence: Not stated: the database is not published as open data, and it holds points of contact
items.check: Checked 2026-10-18. Federal open data give non-PRASA systems by municipio only: ECHO and SDWIS list the municipios each system serves and its owner type (published as counts and residents served, infrastructure_series.json: water_nonprasa, water_nonprasa_pop), with no coordinates. EPA's Community Water System Service Area Boundaries (ORD, 2025) holds 70 Puerto Rico systems, almost all PRASA's. FRS points match 77 of the 404 systems. EPA Region 2 presented a database of the 235 assessed non-PRASA systems with geocoordinates (May 2025) that is not public. Many system names carry a person's or a family's name, so names are never published; counts by barrio would need locations.
items.question: May Foundation for Puerto Rico receive, and publish only as counts and population served by barrio (never names, contacts or points), the locations of the non-PRASA community water systems from the 2022-2024 assessment database? Under what terms?
items.who_to_ask: EPA Region 2, Caribbean Environmental Protection Division; Puerto Rico Department of Health, Drinking Water Program (Programa de Agua Potable)

items.title: Treatment facilities from SAMHSA's live locator (FindTreatment.gov API)
items.why: The locator is updated continuously; the National Directories the observatory uses describe the survey of the year before.
items.source: SAMHSA, FindTreatment.gov locator API (exportsAsJson v2)
items.licence: Not stated: the API guide (version 1.12, 2026-08-17) states no licence and is addressed to 'the approved user'
items.geography: Facility point (published as counts by municipio only)
items.check: Checked 2026-10-18. The API states no licence, and a test query for Puerto Rico returned an empty answer. The observatory uses SAMHSA's 2025 National Directories instead, which carry SAMHSA's Public Domain Notice (community_series.json: bh_*; counts only, no names or points).
items.question: May Foundation for Puerto Rico read the FindTreatment.gov locator API to publish counts of treatment facilities by municipio and type of care (no names, addresses or points)? Does it need approval, and under what terms may the results be republished?
items.who_to_ask: SAMHSA, Behavioral Health Services Information System (BHSIS) project office, through the contact in the FindTreatment.gov API guide

items.title: Reservoir water levels (USGS lake and reservoir gauges)
items.why: Live drought and water-supply signal: how full Carraízo, La Plata and the other reservoirs are, set against rationing, rainfall and the municipalities each one serves.
items.source: USGS Water Data API (monitoring locations of type lake or reservoir, latest continuous values)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-01 without a key: 121 lake or reservoir monitoring locations in Puerto Rico, 81 of them named Lago; of the first 60 Lago sites, 13 reported a reservoir water-surface elevation (parameters 72375, 72376, 72379) on 2026-11-01. Still to do: the full-pool and dead-pool elevation of each reservoir (Army Corps or AAA) so a level can be read as percent full, and which municipalities each reservoir serves. Fits the nightly refresh. Complements the streamflow row (rivers and rain). Live 2026-11-02: reservoirs.geojson, 25 reservoirs (the 19 of AAA's report and 6 others), the latest reading read live by the page, 120 daily values and the usual level of each week (2011-2025). AAA's alert levels not published (no licence stated; written request drafted).

items.title: Vegetation greenness from satellite (Sentinel-2 NDVI)
items.why: Green cover by barrio and how it changes: vegetation loss after hurricanes and drought, recovery, and green space where people live. More frequent and finer than the tree canopy snapshots.
items.source: Copernicus Sentinel-2 Level-2A, read from the open Earth Search catalogue on AWS
items.licence: Copernicus Sentinel data terms: free, full and open use; credit 'Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data [year]'
items.geography: Raster, 10 m (publish barrio and municipio summaries, not images)
items.cadence: Every 5 days (cloud-free composites monthly or seasonal)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-01 without a key: 230 Sentinel-2 L2A scenes over Puerto Rico for September and October 2026; the band files (Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF) download directly. Still to do: the build has no raster reader yet (see landcover); clouds over the Cordillera need composites; decide the summary unit (barrio) and the season. Live 2026-11-04 (terrain and climate step 1, decision 80): vegetation_series.json and vegetation_barrio.json, the median NDVI of a clear-sky median composite of June-September 2024-2026 (984 Sentinel-2 L2A Collection 1 scenes from Earth Search, read at 40 m onto heat.py's 60 m grid), the share of land with dense vegetation (0.6 or more) and with little or none (below 0.2) and the residents on the latter, by municipio and barrio (vegetation.py with raster.py, docs/vegetation.md). Same summers and grid as the Landsat surface heat; across barrios greener is cooler (Spearman -0.89). Change over time (hurricanes, drought) is not built yet.

items.title: A satellite image every 2 to 3 days, 30 m (Harmonized Landsat Sentinel-2, HLS)
items.why: Landsat and Sentinel-2 made into one series, so greenness can be followed through a season: drought, recovery after a storm, and change over time, which the summer composite cannot show.
items.source: NASA HLS v2.0 (HLSL30 and HLSS30), from Microsoft Planetary Computer (hls2-l30, hls2-s30)
items.licence: NASA open data, no restriction on use; credit NASA LP DAAC
items.cadence: Every 2 to 3 days since 2020 on Planetary Computer
items.check: Verified 2026-11-09 without a key: an HLSS30 scene over San Juan (February 2025) read by raster.py (UTM 19N, nodata -9999). Planetary Computer serves it with its anonymous token, so no NASA Earthdata login is needed. Clouds: use the Fmask band and monthly composites.

items.title: Land surface temperature and urban heat islands (Landsat)
items.why: Which barrios are hottest on a clear day, set against tree cover, age and health. Fills the gap the blocked heat row leaves. Landsat passes about 10:30 in the morning, so it shows daytime heat only; night heat is the ecostress-lst row. Step 1 of the terrain and climate proposal (docs/terrain-climate-proposal-2026-11.md).
items.source: USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 surface temperature, read from Microsoft Planetary Computer (anonymous access)
items.licence: US Government work, public domain (cite USGS)
items.geography: Raster, 30 m (100 m thermal, resampled; publish barrio summaries)
items.cadence: Every 8 days with Landsat 8 and 9 (summer composites)
items.check: Verified 2026-11-01 without an account: a Landsat 9 scene of 2026-10-29 found and its thermal band downloaded with Planetary Computer's anonymous token. The AWS copy is requester-pays, so it is not used. Still to do: surface temperature is the ground's, not the air's (label it); clouds; choose dry-season and summer composites; the build has no raster reader yet. Live 2026-11-04 (terrain and climate step 1, decision 80): heat_series.json and heat_barrio.json, the median and 90th-percentile surface temperature of a clear-sky median composite of June-September 2024-2026 (244 scenes, 60 m), the share of land among Puerto Rico's hottest tenth and the residents there, by municipio and barrio (heat.py with raster.py, docs/heat.md). USGS has no surface temperature where ASTER GED lacks emissivity (13.5% of the land, mostly the northwest): heat.py computes it there from the scene's radiance and atmosphere bands, checked against USGS at every build.

items.title: Night and daytime land surface temperature (NASA ECOSTRESS)
items.why: Where surfaces stay hot after dark, when heat harms health most. ECOSTRESS flies on the International Space Station, so it passes at different hours, night included; Landsat (landsat-lst) only sees mid-morning. Step 2 of the terrain and climate proposal (docs/terrain-climate-proposal-2026-11.md).
items.source: NASA ECOSTRESS Level-2 tiled land surface temperature and emissivity (ECO_L2T_LSTE, collection 2), from the LP DAAC
items.licence: NASA Earth science data: no restrictions on use (NASA Earthdata data use policy; cite the product DOI). Download needs a free Earthdata login, which FPR already holds for night lights (to confirm for this product)
items.geography: Raster, 70 m (publish barrio and municipio summaries, not images)
items.cadence: Irregular, several passes a week at varying times since 2018; build seasonal night and day composites
items.check: Checked and built 2026-11-04 (terrain and climate step 2, decision 80): FPR's Earthdata token (decision 75) downloads the product from the LP DAAC's cloud store with no new terms to accept. 295 night granules (21:00-06:00, NASA's NIGHT flag) of June-September 2024-2026, from 47 passes of the space station; masks: QC best or nominal, cloud, water. Live as night_heat_series.json and night_heat_barrio.json (ecostress.py, docs/ecostress.md): the median and 90th-percentile night surface temperature on heat.py's 60 m grid, the share of land among Puerto Rico's warmest tenth at night and the residents there; the typical cell has 13 clear nights. Built in GitHub Actions (ecostress.yml), where the token is a secret. Daytime ECOSTRESS passes are not used: Landsat covers the morning.

items.title: Street-level heat and thermal comfort simulation (PALM-4U)
items.why: Air temperature, wind and the thermal comfort indices PET and UTCI street by street, day and night, which satellites cannot measure: where people feel the heat, and what shade, trees or cool roofs would change. Step 5 of the terrain and climate proposal (docs/terrain-climate-proposal-2026-11.md), for one or two pilot neighbourhoods.
items.source: PALM model system with its urban components (PALM-4U), Leibniz University Hannover, run by a research partner on 3D buildings, trees, surfaces and terrain
items.licence: The model is open source (GNU GPL v3); who owns and may publish the results is set in the partnership agreement (to confirm)
items.geography: Grid of a few metres over a pilot area of a few square kilometres (for example Santurce or Río Piedras)
items.cadence: One-off runs for chosen days (a typical hot day and night), repeated for adaptation scenarios
items.size: large (publish summaries and map tiles of the pilot area)
items.check: Not a download: needs a partner with high-performance computing and PALM experience (a university or research centre), building heights and tree data for the pilot area, and an FPR decision. Results are model output, not measurements: label them and state the simulated day.

items.title: Gridded population by year, 100 m (WorldPop)
items.why: A yearly population surface below the barrio, so exposure to floods, heat or distance to services can be counted for any shape and year, not only for Census years.
items.source: WorldPop (University of Southampton), Global2 constrained population, release R25A
items.check: Verified 2026-11-01 without a key: 16 yearly files for Puerto Rico (2015-2030) in the R25A 100 m release; the licence file says CC BY 4.0. Years after the latest input are projections: label them modelled, not counted. For 2020 the Census blocks stay the reference; use WorldPop only for other years and compare the two before publishing.

items.title: Built-up area and population since 1975 (Global Human Settlement Layer)
items.why: How far the built-up area has spread since 1975, in five-year steps, against population, flood zones and protected lands: the long view of 'what changed'.
items.source: European Commission Joint Research Centre, GHSL (GHS-BUILT-S and GHS-POP, release R2023A)
items.licence: Open data of the European Commission, CC BY 4.0 according to JRC's policy (confirm on the product page)
items.cadence: Every 5 years, 1975 to 2020, with 2025 and 2030 projections
items.check: The JRC open-data folder lists GHS_BUILT_S and GHS_POP releases R2022A and R2023A without a key (tested 2026-11-01). Confirm the licence wording on the product page; the GHSL website did not resolve from this machine. Values before 2000 come from older Landsat and are less reliable.

items.title: 1-metre lidar terrain (USGS 3DEP)
items.why: A sharper terrain model than the 3D view's current tiles: hillshade on the 2D map, slope by barrio for landslide and runoff questions, and better relief in 3D. Two more uses (docs/terrain-climate-proposal-2026-11.md): the climb and steepest grade along the 400 m walks the exposure figures already measure (walknet.py), and a first line-of-sight check from the registered towers (towers row) to each barrio, labelled terrain-only (no trees or buildings, no radio model).
items.source: USGS 3D Elevation Program (3DEP), 1-metre DEM from the Puerto Rico and USVI lidar collection
items.check: Verified 2026-11-01 without a key: The National Map API returns 55 one-metre tiles for a 0.2-degree box around San Juan (project PR_PuertoRicoUSVI_D24). The 3D view already draws terrain and hillshade from the Mapzen/AWS terrain tiles (site/js/twin3d.js), so this is an upgrade, not a gap: low priority.

items.title: Active fires from satellite (NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m)
items.why: Grass and brush fires, most of them in the dry south, by municipio and month, updated daily: when and where they burn, against land cover and homes nearby.
items.source: NASA FIRMS, VIIRS 375 m active fire detections on NOAA-20: yearly country files (no key) and the area API with FPR's MAP_KEY
items.licence: NASA open data (confirm the FIRMS credit line)
items.cadence: Daily, near real time; archive since 2012
items.check: Verified 2026-11-10: the yearly country files for Puerto Rico (viirs-jpss1, NOAA-20) are public with no key, 2018-04 to 2025-12, and tag each detection's type (0 vegetation fire, 2 static land source, 3 offshore); Suomi NPP's run 2012-2025 and stopped feeding FIRMS on 2026-11-02; NOAA-21 has no Puerto Rico yearly files yet. FPR's MAP_KEY is the GitHub Actions secret FIRMS_MAP_KEY (set 2026-11-10); the area API accepts 1 to 5 days per request. Live 2026-11-10 (decision 91, step C): fires_series.json by fires.py (workflow fires.yml): detections by municipio for 2019-2025 (408 in 2019, 103 in 2025; 68% in the dry south and southwest; Salinas most), per 100 km², and the last 12 months (279 from 2025-11-10 to 2026-11-09). Counts only; no point is published.

items.title: Places from Foursquare (FSQ Open Source Places)
items.why: A second source of businesses and places beside Overture, to check coverage, and the dates a place was added or flagged closed: a possible signal of openings and closings by municipio.
items.source: Foursquare Open Source Places (release 2026-01-12)
items.licence: Apache 2.0 (keep the licence text and state changes)
items.size: medium (store counts; points follow the places privacy rules)
items.check: 2026-11-09: now a gated dataset on Hugging Face (contact details asked before download), which needs the project lead's OK. date_closed is when Foursquare flagged a place closed, not when it closed, and is often missing: use only as a rough signal and say so. Every point goes through places_privacy.py like Overture's.

items.title: Very high resolution imagery after disasters (Maxar Open Data, Copernicus EMS)
items.why: Before and after pictures and damage maps for hurricanes Fiona and María and the 2020 earthquakes, as event layers.
items.source: Maxar Open Data Program; Copernicus Emergency Management Service rapid mapping
items.licence: Maxar: CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial); Copernicus EMS: free with credit (confirm per product)
items.check: Still to check: which Puerto Rico events each program covered, whether the Maxar program and its catalogue still run, and Compliance on non-commercial terms. Low priority.

items.title: Home loans by census tract (Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, HMDA)
items.why: Where banks lend for homes and where they do not: loans made and denied, amounts and purpose by census tract, beside income, home values and Opportunity Zones. The observatory has no data on credit.
items.source: Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and FFIEC, HMDA Data Browser
items.licence: US Government work (confirm the statement on the HMDA site)
items.geography: Census tract (each loan row carries its tract)
items.size: medium (13,550 loans made in 2023; store tract counts and sums)
items.check: Published 2026-11-16 (decision 107, step 4; credit.py, docs/credit.md): home loans made, home purchase loans, their amount and the denial share by municipio, 2018-2025, in credit_series.json; counts and sums only, no value under 10 loans or decided applications. Puerto Rico 2025: 14,269 loans made, $2.86 billion. Checked: 2023 equals the Data Browser's own totals (13,550 loans, $2.24 billion). Licence: US Government work (17 U.S.C. 105). Census tracts are not published (the rows describe single borrowers).

items.title: Housing Choice Vouchers by census tract (HUD)
items.why: Where families use rent vouchers, beside the public housing and tax credit housing already on the map: the third large housing subsidy.
items.source: US Department of Housing and Urban Development, open data (ArcGIS)
items.licence: US Government work (confirm in the service's metadata)
items.geography: Census tract (942 rows for Puerto Rico)
items.check: Checked 2026-11-16: the service is HUD's file 'up to 12/2025', and HUD leaves out every tract with 10 or fewer voucher holders. In Puerto Rico 766 of the 942 tracts have no value; the 176 shown hold 5,841 vouchers, while HUD's Public Housing Authorities file counts 26,474 occupied Section 8 units (34,208 authorized) for Puerto Rico's housing authorities. A municipio sum would hold about a fifth of the vouchers and would rank municipios by how many tracts pass the threshold. Not published. HUD's Picture of Subsidized Households gives counts by county, but HUD User refuses scripts (chas-latest row); its ArcGIS copy holds December 2020 tracts only.
items.who_to_ask: HUD Office of Policy Development and Research (HUD User), for a script-readable Picture of Subsidized Households by county

items.title: Drought every week by municipio (US Drought Monitor)
items.why: The heat and vegetation layers are one summer picture. This is a weekly series of how much of each municipio is in drought, to read beside reservoir levels, fires and farm land.
items.source: National Drought Mitigation Center (University of Nebraska-Lincoln), USDA and NOAA
items.licence: Free to use with credit: "Data courtesy of NDMC, via https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu" (droughtmonitor.unl.edu/About/Permission.aspx)
items.geography: Municipio (share of its area in each drought class)
items.check: Published 2026-11-16 (decision 107, step 5, first part; drought.py, docs/drought.md): three yearly datasets by municipio, 2000-2026, in drought_series.json, from every weekly map since 2000-01-04 (the service answers one municipio a request; aoi=72 works with StateStatistics, not CountyStatistics). Worst whole year 2015: 28.5% of Puerto Rico in drought on average. The refresh reads the weekly map and its pull request merges itself when the checks pass. Credit line confirmed: "Data courtesy of NDMC, via https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu".

items.title: Damage FEMA inspectors found in homes, by ZIP code and disaster (Individuals and Households Program)
items.why: The observatory already has the aid FEMA approved for households by municipio. This adds the damage inspectors found, for owners and for renters, and a level below municipio (city and ZIP code).
items.source: FEMA, OpenFEMA (HousingAssistanceOwners; HousingAssistanceRenters)
items.geography: ZIP code and city within a municipio, by disaster
items.check: Checked 2026-11-14, keyless: HousingAssistanceOwners has 15,095 Puerto Rico rows (disaster number, municipio, city, ZIP code, valid registrations, inspected damage, amounts). The renters file was not requested. Some rows hold one registration: add up to municipio or apply a minimum count before publishing (decision 107). Check the totals against housing.fema_ia_amount, which is already published.

items.title: Health care providers by specialty and municipio (NPPES registry)
items.why: How many physicians, dentists, nurses and mental health providers are registered in each municipio, by specialty. The observatory has facilities and shortage designations, but no count of providers by specialty.
items.source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, National Plan and Provider Enumeration System (NPPES)
items.licence: US Government work (public domain); counts only, none from 1 to 9
items.geography: Practice address (municipio by city and ZIP code)
items.size: large (national file; keep Puerto Rico counts only)
items.check: Checked 2026-11-14, keyless: the registry API returned Puerto Rico providers (state=PR) with a practice address and specialty codes. Not checked: the API's paging limit and the size of the monthly file. The rows name people: publish counts by municipio and specialty only, with a minimum count. It is a registry, not a head count: a provider who left Puerto Rico may still be listed, so use the deactivation and last-update fields and say what the count is. Published 2026-11-18 (decision 107, step 8; providers.py, docs/providers.md): 7 provider types by municipio from NPPES_November_2026_V2.zip, read as a stream (the API's pages were not needed). 25,740 active individual providers counted, 99.9% placed in a municipio; 177 cells of 1 to 9 left empty. Physicians: 12,375 registered, 5,406 updated within five years (the range). Registered nurses left out: only nurses who bill need an NPI.

items.title: School results, civil-rights data and degrees by field (Urban Institute Education Data API)
items.why: The observatory counts schools, students and teachers. These files add what students achieve (reading and math proficiency by school), school conditions (Civil Rights Data Collection) and the degrees colleges award by field.
items.source: Urban Institute, Education Data Portal (US Department of Education: EDFacts, CRDC, IPEDS, CCD)
items.licence: Open Data Commons Attribution License (ODC-By 1.0) for the portal; the federal data are public domain
items.check: Checked 2026-11-14, keyless, with fips=72: EDFacts assessments 2018, 836 schools with reading and math proficiency; CRDC directory 2020, 841 schools; IPEDS completions by field 2022, 50,100 rows; CCD directory 2023, 861 schools with latitude and longitude. The graduation-rate call for 2020 answered HTTP 500: test again. Not checked: the newest year of each file. EDFacts gives small schools a range, not a number. Each state and Puerto Rico sets its own test: do not compare proficiency with the states. Drawing school points is decision 107 (c). 2026-11-18 (decision 107, step 7, first part): degrees by field published as degrees_series.json, read straight from NCES's IPEDS files (Urban's portal had no completions after 2021 for Puerto Rico), academic years ending 2015 to 2024. Newest years found: EDFacts proficiency by school 2017-18 (Urban; ED Data Express and the DE's Power BI profile are not readable by a script), CRDC 2021-22. Parts 2 (CRDC) and 3 (proficiency) next. 2026-11-18 (step 7, second part): civil-rights data published as school_conditions_series.json: chronic absence 2017-18 and 2021-22 (45.7% in 2021-22; KIDS COUNT reports 48% around 2022-23), students per counselor, schools with a nurse and with no counselor (2021-22; Puerto Rico's staff items are missing in 2017-18, and first-year teachers in 2021-22). Part 3 (proficiency) next. 2026-11-18 (step 7, third part): proficiency published as proficiency_series.json, 2014-15 to 2018-19 (the portal's 2018 is the school year 2018-19: 836 schools, after the closures; the island's 45.2% in Spanish and 30.2% in math match the Department of Education's 45.1% and 30.1%). All three parts live.

items.title: Species records (GBIF)
items.why: Which plants and animals have been recorded where: the first biodiversity data in the observatory, to read beside protected areas, land use and vegetation.
items.source: Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), from many publishers
items.licence: Differs by dataset: CC0, CC BY 4.0 or CC BY-NC 4.0; cite the download's DOI
items.geography: Point (publish counts by barrio or hexagon)
items.check: Checked 2026-11-14, keyless: 4,279,101 records with country code PR. Keep the CC0 and CC BY datasets, or take Compliance's word on the non-commercial ones (decision 107). Records pile up where observers go (roads, El Yunque, the coast), so a count shows observation effort as much as species: say so. Never draw the exact points of threatened species.

items.title: Sea ports and cargo (US Army Corps of Engineers, through NTAD)
items.why: The map has airports and ferries but no cargo ports, and most of Puerto Rico's goods arrive by sea.
items.source: US Army Corps of Engineers, Waterborne Commerce Statistics; BTS National Transportation Atlas Database
items.check: 2026-11-14: BTS's service NTAD_Hazard_Exposure_Principal_Ports (marked BETA) lists San Juan, Guayama and Guaynabo. The Principal Ports service with tonnage was not found under the name tried. Find it and confirm the tonnage fields and the year.

items.title: Flood insurance policies and claims (National Flood Insurance Program)
items.why: How many homes in flood zones are insured and what past floods paid out: the gap between flood exposure and flood insurance.
items.source: FEMA, OpenFEMA (redacted NFIP policies and claims)
items.check: 2026-11-14: the addresses tried (v2/FimaNfipClaims and v2/FimaNfipPolicies) answered 'Page not found', and OpenFEMA's dataset list returned no dataset whose name starts with FimaNfip. Find where FEMA publishes these files now and confirm Puerto Rico rows.

items.title: Births, deaths and net migration by municipio
items.why: Why each municipio gains or loses people: more deaths than births, or people moving away.
items.source: US Census Bureau Population Estimates; Departamento de Salud (vital statistics)
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.check: 2026-11-14: the Vintage 2025 folders for municipios hold population and its change only (prm-est2025-pop.xlsx, prm-est2025-chg.xlsx) and an age-and-sex folder (datasets/2020-2025/puerto-rico/asrh). No file of births, deaths or migration by municipio was seen; the island-level components file was not opened. The Department of Health's figures are under terms that bar republishing (doh-biostatistics row). Net migration by age can be estimated from the age-and-sex files (derived-net-migration-age row).

items.title: Chronic conditions and Medicare spending by municipio (CMS Geographic Variation)
items.why: A health-outcome source that may cover Puerto Rico by municipio: CDC PLACES excludes it and the Department of Health's files cannot be republished. It covers people with Medicare only.
items.source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services
items.check: Not tested. Confirm that the county file has Puerto Rico municipios, which measures it carries for them and that the download needs no key. Most Puerto Rico beneficiaries are in Medicare Advantage (the observatory publishes the share), which fee-for-service figures leave out: check what the file counts before using it.

items.title: Share of income spent on energy, by census tract (DOE LEAD tool)
items.why: Energy burden by income group and housing type, beside the electricity-bill data the observatory already has.
items.source: US Department of Energy, Low-Income Energy Affordability Data (LEAD) tool
items.check: Not tested. Confirm Puerto Rico coverage, the year of the ACS data behind it and a keyless download address. The figures are modelled from the ACS, not measured bills: label them as estimates.

items.title: Veterans Affairs spending by municipio (VA GDX)
items.why: Compensation, pensions, medical care and education benefits paid in each municipio, beside the federal awards already shown.
items.source: US Department of Veterans Affairs, Geographic Distribution of VA Expenditures (GDX)
items.check: Not tested. Confirm that the yearly workbook lists Puerto Rico municipios and downloads without a key. Check for overlap with the USAspending figures already published before adding the two up.

items.title: Beach water quality monitoring (EPA BEACON)
items.why: Which beaches are tested for bacteria and how often they exceed the standard: the first coastal water-quality data, for residents and for the visitor economy.
items.source: US Environmental Protection Agency, BEACON; Departamento de Recursos Naturales y Ambientales
items.check: Not tested. Confirm Puerto Rico beaches, the newest year, and a keyless way to read the data.

items.title: Tsunami evacuation zones
items.why: A coastal hazard the map does not show: flood zones and sea level rise are there, tsunami zones are not.
items.source: Red Sísmica de Puerto Rico (UPR Mayagüez); NOAA National Tsunami Hazard Mitigation Program
items.check: Not tested. Find a machine-readable copy and its terms. If none is stated, ask the Red Sísmica in writing (no request is sent without the project lead's word).

items.title: Rainfall by month and year, gridded (CHIRPS; Daymet)
items.why: Rainfall for every barrio and every year, where the rain gauges cover points only: wet and dry years beside drought, reservoirs, landslides and vegetation.
items.source: Climate Hazards Center, UC Santa Barbara (CHIRPS); NASA ORNL DAAC (Daymet)
items.licence: To confirm for each (CHIRPS states public domain; Daymet is NASA open data)
items.geography: Raster, about 5 km (CHIRPS) and 1 km (Daymet); store summaries by barrio and municipio
items.check: Not tested. Confirm that each covers Puerto Rico and its licence, compare both with the USGS rain gauges already on the map, and pick one. Cells of 5 km are coarse for small barrios: say so.

items.title: More ACS tables: English ability, nutrition assistance, poverty by age
items.why: Dimensions the observatory lacked, from a source it already reads: people who speak English less than "very well" (B16004), households that received nutrition assistance (B22010) and poverty of children and of people 65 and older (B17001).
items.source: US Census Bureau ACS 5-year table files
items.licence: US Government work; cite the Census Bureau as the source
items.geography: Municipio; barrio and census tract for English ability and nutrition assistance
items.check: Published 2026-11-14 (decision 107, step 1; docs/small-area.md, section 10): population.acs_english_lt_very_well_pct and population.acs_pan_hh_pct for the municipios, the barrios and the census tracts; population.acs_child_poverty_pct and population.acs_senior_poverty_pct for the municipios only, because below them the share is flagged less reliable for more than half of the barrios. Households with no vehicle were already published (economy.no_vehicle_hh_pct, since 2026-10-06): this row named them by mistake when it was written. The Puerto Rico questionnaire asks about the Nutritional Assistance Program (PAN), not SNAP.

items.title: Social Security beneficiaries and benefits by ZIP code
items.why: One of the largest federal payments to households in Puerto Rico, by place: retired and disabled workers and survivors, and the monthly benefits paid.
items.source: Social Security Administration, OASDI Beneficiaries by State and ZIP Code
items.check: Checked 2026-11-14: ssa.gov answered HTTP 403 to a plain request for the Puerto Rico workbook (oasdi_zip/2024/pr.xlsx). Not bypassed, so the address itself is not confirmed. Download by hand or ask for a copy a script can read.
items.who_to_ask: Social Security Administration, Office of Research, Evaluation, and Statistics

items.title: Daytime population by municipio (calculated)
items.why: How many people are in each municipio on a working day: residents, plus workers who come in, minus workers who leave. It shows which municipios fill up and which empty out, for services, transit and emergency planning.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.check: Published 2026-11-14 (decision 107, step 1; commuting.py, docs/commuting.md) as commuting_series.json: commuting.daytime_population, commuting.daytime_change_pct and commuting.work_elsewhere_pct, with margins of error. Kind: calculated (an identity, no model): the Census Bureau's formula for the commuter-adjusted population, with the residents of the 2020 Census and the commuting flows of 2016-2020 read from the Census Bureau's table. It counts workers only, not students, shoppers or visitors.

items.title: Public facilities and main roads inside hazard zones (overlaid)
items.why: The observatory counts residents and homes in flood, sea level rise and landslide zones, but not the fire and police stations, libraries, city halls, power plants, bridges, airports and main roads that stand in them.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.geography: Point and road stretch; counts by municipio and barrio
items.check: Published 2026-11-16 (decision 107, step 3; facility_exposure.py, docs/facility-exposure.md): 17 municipio datasets in facility_exposure_series.json, public schools as a map layer and hazard flags in every facility pop-up. In Puerto Rico 327 of 2,274 facilities stand in FEMA's 1% flood area, 17 in NOAA's 3 ft sea level rise area and 26 on High or higher landslide susceptibility land (main island); 27,178 public school students in the flood area; 596.3 km of main road in the flood area and 474.3 km on high landslide land. Kind: overlaid. Bridges and 234 stacked points (several facilities at one address) are not tested.

items.title: Road distance to the nearest supermarket, pharmacy, bank, library and fire station, by barrio (estimate)
items.why: The USDA food-access atlas excludes Puerto Rico (food-access row). The observatory can measure access itself, as it does for hospitals and health centers.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its inputs: Overture (CDLA Permissive 2.0, some ODbL), OpenStreetMap (ODbL), USAC and USGS (public domain), Census (US Government work)
items.check: Published 2026-11-18 (decision 107, step 6; essentials.py, docs/essentials.md): road distance to a supermarket, any food store, a pharmacy, a bank or cooperativa, a library and a fire or EMS station, and residents more than 5 km from a supermarket, for 78 municipios, Puerto Rico and 901 barrios. Check: of OpenStreetMap's places, 76.0% of 292 supermarkets, 87.1% of 387 pharmacies, 84.1% of 308 banks have an Overture place within 300 m. Island: supermarket 2.81 km, pharmacy 2.24 km, bank 3.44 km. FDIC branches were not used for points: half sit at the centre of their ZIP code.

items.title: Residents who can be cut off by road (estimate)
items.why: Where every road out of a community crosses a flood zone or a bridge in poor condition, a storm can isolate it. After Hurricane María many communities were cut off for weeks.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its inputs: OpenStreetMap (ODbL); FEMA, FHWA and Census (US Government works)
items.geography: Census block, summed by barrio and municipio
items.check: Published 2026-11-20 (decision 107, step 9, third part; cutoff.py, docs/cutoff.md): the share of residents with no open road to a hospital when the roads in FEMA's 1% flood area close, when the bridges in poor condition or closed close, and both, for 78 municipios, Puerto Rico and 901 barrios. Island: 16.2% by floods (range 14.9% to 24.5%), 0.1% by bridges. Check: of the 8 WCRP communities whose plans say floods or a failing bridge leave them cut off, 5 have half or more of the residents within 800 m cut off in the model (59.4% on average), against 16 of the other 67 WCRP communities (27.7%). It misses Mariana (Humacao), Punta Tuna (Maunabo), Río Blanco (Naguabo). A hospital is the test, not the town centre: a town centre in the flood area is often itself cut off. Landslides are not in the model.

items.title: Months for night-time light to return after Hurricanes María and Fiona, by barrio (calculated)
items.why: The observatory holds night-time light for every barrio and month since 2012 but does not yet read recovery from it: how deep the loss was after each storm and how long light took to come back.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its input: NASA Black Marble (CC0, cite the product) and the Census outlines (US Government work, no US copyright)
items.check: Published 2026-11-17 (decision 107, step 5, second part; storm_recovery.py, docs/storm_recovery.md): months until light came back and the darkest month, for María (2017) and Fiona (2022), 78 municipios, Puerto Rico and 901 barrios, in storm_recovery_series.json and storm_recovery_barrio.json. Rule chosen: 80% of the same month the year before, two months in a row (90% for three months, the first idea, gives the island 14 months after María against about 8 in the restoration record). Check: by the rule the island's light was back by 2018-05 after María; the Army Corps of Engineers reported 98.4% of the utility's customers restored in mid-May 2018. After Fiona it was back by 2022-10; LUMA reported 90% of customers restored on 2022-10-01. EAGLE-I's outage record (Oak Ridge National Laboratory, CC BY 4.0, figshare 24237376, 2022 file) agrees by region: in each of the seven LUMA regions the customers out fell to 10% of the peak or fewer between 2022-09-29 (San Juan, Bayamón, Carolina) and 2022-10-10 (Mayagüez), the southwest last, so every region was mostly back within October.

items.title: One hexagon grid for every layer: residents, buildings, heat, slope, flood and broadband by H3 hexagon
items.why: Barrios differ a great deal in size. One grid of equal cells lets layers be crossed below barrio in the same unit, the one the broadband layer already uses.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.geography: Equal-area hexagon of 1 km² (the map's own grid, core/hexbin.js)
items.check: Kind: calculated for surfaces (heat, slope, vegetation, flood share: averages per cell) and modelled for residents (census block residents spread over building footprints). Inputs already held: census blocks, building footprints, the 60 m surfaces, flood.geojson and broadband_hex.geojson. Check: the hexagons' residents must add up to the block and barrio totals. Hexagons with few residents get a minimum count, as the broadband layer's 10-location floor. Loads on demand so the map's script budget does not grow. 2026-11-19 (step 9, first part): hex_grid.geojson published with residents, housing units, buildings, land under buildings and residents in the flood area for 8,745 hexagons; the cells add up exactly to the island totals. Changed from the plan: the observatory's own equal-area hexagons of 1 km², not H3 (H3 cells vary in area; the FCC gives only the H3 cell of each location, so broadband stays on its own layer). 2026-11-20 (step 9, second part): each hexagon also holds the median summer-morning surface temperature and the median greenness (NDVI) of its 60 m cells, and the mean slope of its 10 m cells; 653 hexagons of land with no resident or building were added so the three cover the island (9,398 cells).

items.title: Net migration by age group and municipio (estimate)
items.why: No file gives migration by municipio (vital-components row). It can be solved for: the people of an age group five years later, minus those expected to survive, is the net number who moved.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its inputs: Census Bureau (US Government work), UN World Population Prospects (CC BY 3.0 IGO)
items.check: Published 2026-11-24 (decision 107, step 9, sixth part; netmig_age.py, docs/net-migration-age.md): net migration by age between the 2010 and 2020 censuses for 78 municipios and Puerto Rico, by the residual method. Island, ages 10 and over: -384,100 (-11.3% of expected); ages 20 to 29, -28.1%. Check: the residual for every age (ages 10 and over, -384,100, plus about -44,868 children born in the decade) is -428,968, 6.1% from the demographic balance of the two censuses (-456,866: the change in population minus births plus deaths). The UN's net migration for 2010-2019 is -408,407; the Census Bureau's estimate made before the 2020 census, -583,765, overstated the loss.

items.title: What lies upstream of each reservoir and river gauge (overlaid)
items.why: 'What drains here' answers for one clicked point. The same catchments can give, for every reservoir and gauge, the residents, buildings, wastewater plants and protected land upstream of it.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its inputs: USGS, EPA and Census (US Government works), Overture buildings (ODbL)
items.geography: Reservoir and gauge (point), with its upstream area
items.check: Published 2026-11-23 (decision 107, step 9, fourth part; upstream.py, docs/upstream.md, Reservoirs page section 4): for 25 reservoirs and 71 river gauges, the land that drains to each and the residents, housing units, buildings, wastewater treatment plants in force (EPA POTW) and protected land on it. Check: 73 of the 87 sites with a USGS drainage area are within 25% of it (median ratio 1.03); the rest are marked. Six off-stream reservoirs (fed by canals or pumps) have no figures. Building it found that the catchment network linked river mouths along the coast; watersheds.py now stops at each river's last reach, which also fixes What drains here near the coast. Impaired waters were not added (EPA ATTAINS is not in the cache).

items.title: Jobs within 30 and 45 minutes by road, by municipio (estimate)
items.why: Jobs are published where they are; this shows how many a resident can reach, which is what matters for work.
items.source: Observatory, computed from files it already publishes
items.licence: Follows its inputs: BLS QCEW and Census (US Government works), Overture (CDLA Permissive 2.0, some ODbL), OpenStreetMap (ODbL)
items.check: Published 2026-11-24 (decision 107, step 9, fifth part; jobs_reach.py, docs/jobs-reach.md): the jobs residents can reach within 30 and 45 minutes by car, and their share of Puerto Rico's jobs, for 78 municipios and Puerto Rico. Island: 236,860 jobs within 30 minutes, 371,661 within 45 (QCEW 2025: 943,002 jobs). Check: in the Census Bureau's commuting flows of 2016-2020, 95.9% of the workers who live and work in Puerto Rico work in a municipio within 45 minutes of theirs in the model (92.3% of those who work in another municipio). QCEW has no jobs below the municipio: they are spread over business places, and only municipio figures are published.
